articles.text: Piedmont students, parents, teachers and community members braved the threat of rain Tuesday morning at 7:45 a.m. to honor the legacy of civil rights icon Ruby Bridges. Hundreds of Piedmonters showed up at Piedmont Park for Ruby Bridges Walk to School Day to learn about Bridges’ efforts as a six-year-old in 1960 to help end segregation in her New Orleans school by simply walking to school. Nationwide participation in the event has increased steadily since 2018 when fifth graders in South San Francisco decided to emulate Ruby and spotlight her bravery by walking to school in unity. “The event was amazing, we had an immense turnout,” said Jean Takazawa, PHS Director of Diversity Equity and Inclusion (DEI). Photo by Jean Takazawa Hundred of people showed up at Piedmont Park early Tuesday morning, November 14, for Ruby Bridges Walk to School Day.

articles.text: Designer Walter Hood hosted an event at the Alan Harvey Theater on Tuesday, November 7, to announce the beginning of the design phase for the newly announced Sidney & Irene Dearing Memorial in Piedmont. The memorial would be located in Triangle Park at the intersection of Magnolia and Wildwood Avenues, near the home the Dearings owned in the 1920s. Mayor Cavenaugh briefly discussed the history of the project, including the City Council’s decision to create a memorial at Triangle Park, the Park Commission’s discussions with relatives of Sidney and Irene Dearing, and the City’s selection of Hood Design Studio to create a fitting memorial. Walter Hood took attendees on a virtual tour of projects he has designed, discussing the creative process that led to each design. A few of the projects he highlighted included 7th Street Dancing Lights in West Oakland, the San Bernadino “Curtain of Courage” memorializing victims of the December 2015 domestic terrorist acts, the John Robinson Jr. Town Square in Arlington, VA, and the African Ancestors Memorial Garden at the International African American Museum in Charleston, SC. After the talk, Hood joined guests at a reception in the lobby. “Based on the audience’s reactions, the lecture was very well received,” said Yao Liu, a member of Hood Design Studio. “People seem to be looking forward to working with us on this project.” Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that he was “definitely impressed” by the presentation. “It really demonstrates Photo by Echa Schneider Walter Hood, designer and chair of UC Berkeley’s Department of Landscape Architecture & Environmental Planning, gives a presentation at Alan Harvey Theater on the newly announced Sidney Dearing memorial. the level of expertise that Hood Design Studio brings to the project and to the city. We’re looking forward to working with them on next steps.” Hood Design Studio is an award-winning social art and design practice located in Oakland, CA, helmed by Creative Director Walter Hood, who readers may recognize as the current Chair of UC Berkeley’s Department of Landscape Architecture & Environmental Planning. Among other things accolades, Hood is a recipient of the 2017 Academy of Arts and Letters Architecture Award, 2019 Knight Public Spaces Fellowship, 2019 MacArthur Fellowship (the “Genius Grant”), 2019 Dorothy and Lillian Gish Prize, and the 2021 recipient of the Architectural Leagues’ President’s Medal. 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall City Editor: Jay Russell PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Matt Simons Ed Gilligan Will Becker (intern) Micah Temple (intern) Clea Villaluz (intern) SCHOOLS Ada Cliff SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: Camille Parker was born Camille Jabbie (pronounced JayBee) on November 9, 1926 in Amite, Louisiana. She recently died at her home in Castro Valley. The last lines of the obituary written by her son read, “Camille and Warren (her husband) enjoyed their children, grand-children and great grand-children. She was called home on September 1, 2023 at 96 years old after a long life well lived.” At her burial I built her eulogy around three words. Smile, Sunshine and Supplication. Camille had a beautiful, light-up-theroom, brighten your day smile. When she smiled the world instantly became a better place. For many years Camille was the Sunshine Chairperson of her Sunday School Class. This meant she sent get well-cards, birthday cards and thinking-of-you cards. It meant she called those who were absent, listened to those who were down, and comforted those who were grieving. It was her ministry to be a ray of sunshine – and she shined brightly. Supplication is to offer prayers for the well-being of others. There are many who were greatly helped by the knowledge that Camille was praying on their behalf. Her supplication was diligent, consistent and heartfelt. When Camille said, “I will pray for you,” it was more than a nicety – it was a promise. articles.text: Photos by Anne Hauss Davies Piedmont Scouts in Troop 4 help load donated food onto a truck during the annual Scouting for Food Drive. Pictured are: (front) Rohan Seshan (left), Niko Wolff, Felix Kansal; (back) Jerry Yu, Scoutmaster Arvind Seshan, Naomi Treichler, Joelle Frechette, and Assistant Scoutmaster Dante Rodriguez. On Saturday, November 11 at 8:30 AM, a truck from the Alameda County Community Food Bank lumbered into the parking lot at Community Hall. A half hour later a very busy day began, as Piedmont Scouts went door to door throughout the city as part of their annual Scouting for Food drive. Just like every year, the Scouts tackled the herculean task through a mixture of meticulous planning and selfless teamwork. Last week Piedmont Cub Scouts placed door hanger reminders on houses throughout the city, and on Saturday the older Scouts picked up bags of donated food city-wide. “It was a big task,” said Anne Hauss Davies, a member of the Piedmont Council Executive Board and chair for Scouting for Food. “Some troops had difficulty recruiting enough Scouts given the holiday weekend but thankfully other troops pitched in and we finished up just after noon.” Hauss Davies said that the Food Bank’s truck driver estimated the Scouts collected about 8,000 pounds of food, far more than last year’s total of 7,000 pounds. In addition, the Scouting for Food virtual food drive has raised about $3,500 in donations so far. “1 in 5 people in Alameda County are food insecure, and Piedmont has a lot to offer the community. The Food Bank is a wonderful avenue for Piedmont to give because its great purchasing power means they will be able to buy food at prices unavailable to other organizations. Basically, our money will go a lot farther at the food bank.” Scouting for Food’s virtual food drive is open until Thursday, November 30. articles.text: Piedmonters gearing up for the Christmas season will be happy to know that the Piedmont Scout Council’s Christmas tree Lot will be opening on Saturday, November 25 in the parking lot of Coaches Field. Community members looking to add a festive touch to their homes this holiday season will be able to buy trees, wreaths, garlands, tree stands, and mistletoe from the lot for pick-up and delivery. The tree Lot is also accepting online pre-orders at www.scouttreelot.org. Delivery service will be available throughout Piedmont and select neighborhoods in Oakland beginning the weekend of November 25. “I think it’s just one of those holiday traditions that people support because we’re a good cause,” said Tom Smegal, head of the tree lot volunteer committee. This will be his fourth year running the tree lot, although Smegal has been volunteering there since he was a scout himself. “The folks that we’re supporting are the youth programs for our scouts, our Cub Scouts, our venturing clubs, the Piedmont Community Service Crew, and others. It’s a good cause.” Smegal also asserted that there is something special about buying your tree from a local lot like their own. “When you’re up there at the tree lot, picking out a tree and have a fourth grader in a Cub Scout uniform that’s helping you pick out that 10-foot tree, it’s a fun experience – almost reminiscent of when you were a child. It’s the kind of thing that brings together families and creates family memories,” said Smegal. The Scout Tree Lot sells three kinds of trees: Noble firs, which are their most popular, tend to have a lot of branch definition while maintaining a delightfully bushy shape; Silver tips, which are taller and thinner and great for hanging large amounts of ornaments; and Douglas firs, the easiest to care for. They have a sweet fragrance to their needles when crushed. The Scout Tree Lot has been highly successful in previous years. In 2022, sales were high, generating as much as $50,000 on its opening weekend with an additional $30,000 in online sales before opening day. The tree lot will be open until the third weekend in December or until the lot sells out its entire stock. “Whichever comes first,” said Smegal. “Although, we usually sell out in mid-December.” Staff Photo Piedmont Community Service Crew members are shown volunteering at last year’s Piedmont Scout Tree Lot: Dave Feinberg (left), Ashley Ronen, PCSC Advisor Ken Li, Samantha Ronen, Ishaia Goldberg-Berman, Bruno Banuelos, Kyra Dang, and Holland Feinberg. “When I was an executive,I used to carry my lunch in a fancy briefcase, too.”

articles.text: More than meets the rye Bread – in all its forms – is a common food in many households. There are several methods to make bread but a common one involves the use of yeast. The process of making bread with yeast is a cool way to examine and experience science at home – not to mention that it’s delicious. What you knead to know Bread is a type of food that has existed throughout human history. Across different cultures bread appears in many different shapes and names. For example, flatbread is one of the oldest forms of bread. Versions of flatbread have existed in the Middle East, Africa, Europe, and beyond for thousands of years. Like most types of bread, flatbread is made with simple ingredients such as flour, milk or water, and salt. However, other kinds of bread use ingredients such as yeast to create bread that is fluffier and softer than flatbread. A feast for yeast So, what exactly is yeast and what is its function in the process of making bread? Yeast is defined as a single-cell, fungal microorganism, which basically means it is a very small form of life – like moss or mold. There are different types of yeast that exist around us, but the yeast that is added to bread is known simply as baker’s yeast. Bread is an example of how science is all around us Baker’s yeast often comes in a dried form and is added to dough to make it rise and create bread with an airy texture. In order to make bread rise, dried yeast first needs two important things: warmth and sugar. Yeast needs warmth in order for it to do its job in bread. Warm water is often used with dried yeast to raise it to a temperature where it can work well. Also, just like all living things, yeast needs food in order to function – specifically sugar. In bread dough, there are lots of sugars for the yeast to eat – in the flour and any other added sugars. As it eats the sugar, yeast creates a chemical called carbon dioxide which creates many small air bubbles in bread dough and causes it to rise. This process is called fermentation. Once the fermentation process is completed, the dough can go into the oven to bake. The yeast that was used in the dough creates an airy and light texture in the baked bread – a tasty result thanks to science. Last but not yeast! You may have thought that there isn’t much science in bread, but without chemical or biological reactions the loaf of bread on your dinner table would look a lot different. Bread is just another small example of how science is all around us – even in places we would least expect it. Cameron Schneider is with Chabot Space & Science Center, a non-profit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement, located in the Oakland hills. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the universe and planet Earth.
articles.title: Science is all around us, especially on the holidays

There are several methods to make bread but a common one involves the use of yeast. The process of making bread with yeast is a cool way to examine and experience science at home – not to mention that it’s delicious. What you knead to know Bread is a type of food that has existed throughout human history. Across different cultures bread appears in many different shapes and names. For example, flatbread is one of the oldest forms of bread. Versions of flatbread have existed in the Middle East, Africa, Europe, and beyond for thousands of years. Like most types of bread, flatbread is made with simple ingredients such as flour, milk or water, and salt. However, other kinds of bread use ingredients such as yeast to create bread that is fluffier and softer than flatbread. A feast for yeast So, what exactly is yeast and what is its function in the process of making bread? Yeast is defined as a single-cell, fungal microorganism, which basically means it is a very small form of life – like moss or mold. There are different types of yeast that exist around us, but the yeast that is added to bread is known simply as baker’s yeast. Bread is an example of how science is all around us Baker’s yeast often comes in a dried form and is added to dough to make it rise and create bread with an airy texture. In order to make bread rise, dried yeast first needs two important things: warmth and sugar. Yeast needs warmth in order for it to do its job in bread. Warm water is often used with dried yeast to raise it to a temperature where it can work well. Also, just like all living things, yeast needs food in order to function – specifically sugar. In bread dough, there are lots of sugars for the yeast to eat – in the flour and any other added sugars. As it eats the sugar, yeast creates a chemical called carbon dioxide which creates many small air bubbles in bread dough and causes it to rise. This process is called fermentation. Once the fermentation process is completed, the dough can go into the oven to bake. The yeast that was used in the dough creates an airy and light texture in the baked bread – a tasty result thanks to science. Last but not yeast! You may have thought that there isn’t much science in bread, but without chemical or biological reactions the loaf of bread on your dinner table would look a lot different. Bread is just another small example of how science is all around us – even in places we would least expect it. articles.text: Foreign language classes at Piedmont High School displayed their talents in the amphitheater on Monday, November 13, for the World Language Singing Competition. Each foreign language class performed a song they learned in their target language, and engaged in friendly competition with other French, Mandarin and Spanish language students. Period 7 Honors Spanish 4 students ended their performance by tossing roses and flower petals in the air. Staff Photos Eleventh grader Clare Weiss, a member of the All-State Jazz Choir, led her class, Honors Spanish 4, with a remarkable solo. Students and faculty members enjoyed the warm mid-November weather on November 13 for outdoor singing. Period 7 Mandarin class students strike poses at the end of their song and dance. Period 6, AP Chinese punctuated notes in their song with the snapping sound of opening red fans. Period 6 AP Spanish’s song and dance narrowly beat out AP Chinese to win the period. Each song and dance began with an introduction of the class to a large crowd on hand. Many students were allowed out of class to see the performances, which included choreography, matching outfits, and instrumental music. The competition’s origin can be traced back to 2017 when PHS French teacher Christele David, brought her French classes to other foreign language classrooms to serenade them with French carols. articles.text: On the first weekend in November, 15 Scouts and parents from Piedmont’s Troop 1 embarked on an overnight kayaking trip on Tomales Bay. Carrying all of their tents and camping supplies in two-person kayaks, the Scouts set off on a five-mile journey, paddling along the western side of Tomales Bay to their campsite. On the journey the Scouts saw multiple stingrays, many seals, a few otters, and hundreds of jellyfish – some of which even ended up in the kayaks. The weather was wet and damp, but the Scouts enjoyed a campfire and storytelling as night fell. A few Scouts and adults kayaked late at night to see bioluminescence – a phenomenon visible on Tomales Bay only on moonless nights in the late summer and early fall. It is a time when microorganisms give off light if they are physically disturbed. The Scouts formed eerie, glowing white clouds by agitating the water with a paddle. Rain the next morning didn’t dampen their spirits as they packed their supplies and prepared for the trip home. articles.text: Faith Chin wins singles, Hallie Burden third From first-time racket holders to remarkable wins, Piedmont’s JV Tennis Team has had an extraordinary season, culminating with the 9th annual Western Alameda County Conference Junior Varsity Jamboree on Saturday, October 28 at Castro Valley High School. The Highlanders finished second of eight schools in team competition with a 22-12 overall record in the tournament. Piedmont had the best record in performances by its single matches, winning 15 of 20 matches. Faith Chin won the singles bracket, defeating Bishop O’Dowd’s Sonja Abid in a hard-earned, 7-6 (7-5) tiebreaker victory. Hallie Burden came away with a decisive third-place win over O’Dowd’s Penny Wong, 6-2. The JV tennis team’s journey this season was more than just wins and losses; it was about building lasting friendships, pushing boundaries, and nurturing a love for the game. The young athletes displayed unwavering dedication, sportsmanship, and teamwork. Piedmont placed second at the WACC JV Jamboree on October 28. articles.text: Olympic rower Scott Gault is inducted into the Olympic Club Hall of Fame in San Francisco. On October 12, Piedmont High alum Scott Gault was inducted into the Olympic Club Hall of Fame in San Francisco. At Piedmont High he played football, basketball and golf, but his world changed when he began rowing with the Oakland Stokes in his senior year. It led him to the University of Washington, where he spent four years in one of the nation’s premier rowing programs, while earning a degree in Industrial Engineering. After college, he joined the U.S. national team and helped bring home the gold medal in the men’s quadruple sculls at the 2008 Rowing World Cup in Lucerne, Switzerland. In 2008 he finished 5th in the Beijing Olympic Games. Gault eventually switched events to the men’s coxless four and qualified for the 2012 Olympic team. In the 2012 Olympics in London, he and his teammates had never competed together internationally, but they won the Bronze Medal, missing the gold by 3.5 seconds. Gault now spends his time on his other passions. He has played for more than a decade in the Olympic Club basketball league. He is also a pilot, cyclist and skier. He is raising his family in Marin County and currently a Senior Vice President at Newfront Insurance specializing in aviation insurance. Scott Gault with niece Henley Azad, who was named in his honor when she was born on opening night of the London Olympics.

articles.text: A new exhibit at San Francisco’s Museum of the African Diaspora featuring work by local artist Salimatu Amabebe is on view now through December 10. The exhibition, entitled SON, is Amabebe’s first solo museum exhibit and is co-curated by the artist and Key Jo Lee, Chief of Curatorial Affairs and Public Programs at MoAD. A mabebe is a Niger ian-American chef and multimedia artist based in Oakland. He is the founder and director of “Black Feast,” a culinary event that celebrates Black artists and writers through food. His work primarily focuses on the intersection of food and art, drawing from family memories, Nigerian recipes and Black culinary history. In SON, the artist explores the relationship between home, memory, and metamorphosis by transforming an area of the museum with haunting red hues. Amabebe’s solo exhibition is the third of MoAD’s Emerging Artists Program series. Visit https://www.moadsf. org/exhibitions/salimatu-amabebe-grass to learn more. The works of artist Salimatu Amabebe are now on view at the Museum of African Diaspora.
articles.title: Salimatu Amabebe exhibit at MoAD on view through Dec. 10

articles.text: December tickets for San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s (SF MOMA) Infinite Love, the highly anticipated and widely popular exhibition by artist Yayoi Kusama, are on sale now. The vibrant and immersive exhibition opened in October and tickets sold fast, but the museum is now offering tickets to visit in December. January tickets will be released December 5 for members and December 7 to the general public. Yayoi Kusama is one of the most iconic and globally celebrated artists working today, known for her use of mirrors and bright colors. The artist’s first solo presentation in Northern California encompasses two infinity mirror rooms in the museum, including her newest room, Dreaming of Earth’s Sphericity, I Would Offer My Love (2023), a kaleidoscope color and light. Love is Calling (2013) is the second room in the presentation and one of Kusama’s largest and most immersive works. The exhibition features a darkened environment lit up by vividly colored inflatable forms that extend from the floor and ceiling, accompanied by the sound of the artist reciting a poem about love. All tickets for Kusama exhibitions are timed. Visit https:// www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/ yayoi-kusama-infinite-love/ to learn more.
articles.title: Yayoi Kusama exhibit now on view at SF MOMA

articles.text: Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) curators and staff will host a gallery chat this Saturday, November 18, between 1 p.m. and 3 p.m. The event is designed to mimic a guided tour but with an opportunity to chat with and ask questions of the museum’s curators. The museum is encouraging meaningful conversations and fresh interpretations to connect with the artwork, artifacts, and stories in our galleries. Visitors may view and discuss with staff the museum’s newest exhibition, Por el Pueblo: The Legacy and Influence of Malaquías Montoya, which opened last month in the museum’s Great Hall. Montoya often uses political imagery in his work and has produced substantial art centered around the issue of immigration. His posters, graphic prints, and murals often highlighted political and social justice issues, and have helped define the Chicano identity and culture for nearly fifty years. Curators will be onsite on Saturday afternoon to answer questions about this important body of work. Gallery chats will take place every Saturday from 1 to 3 p.m. and are included with Museum and Special Exhibition admission. No reservation necessary. Visit https://museumca.org/ event/gallery-chats-at-omcanov-18/ to learn more about this new OMCA feature. Oakland Museum curators and staff will be onsite every Saturday between 1 and 3 p.m.
articles.title: Oakland Museum curators to host gallery chat on Sat.

articles.text: Shotguns Players’ newest Tony Award-winning production Hedwig and the Angry Inch is playing onstage at the Ashby Theatre in Berkeley now through December 17. Written by John Cameron Mitchell and directed by Richard Mosqueda, the play is adapted from the off-Broadway theater hit of the same name, later made into a movie in 2001. Hedwig and the Angry Inch follows German emigrant Hedwig, who is the victim of a botched sex-change operation. The current adaptation takes place in a seedy dive bar in Berkeley. Hedwig is an international song stylist and East German rock ‘n’ roll goddess. This outrageous play is performed by Pangaea Colter in the form of a rock gig and stand-up comedy routine backed by a hard-rocking band. Mosqueda said the inspiration came from their first viewing of the film back in a high school English class. “A crudely drawn animation played on the screen detailing a story about the origin of humans, Pangaea Colter plays the role of Hedwig in the Shotgun Players production of Hedwig and the Angry Inch. originally three genders, who were once attached and then separated, now looking for the other half. An androgynous blonde bombshell appeared on the screen wailing to the heavens. I was glued to the television. And as a deeply closeted queer kid, I felt seen, if only for a moment,” Mosqueda said. Lyrics and music are by Stephen Trask. To view showtimes and to purchase tickets, visit https://shotgunplayers.org/Online/default. asp.

articles.text: Piedmont Center for the Arts marks the 11th year of its Berkeley Symphony and Friends chamber music series with a concert on Sunday, November 19 at 4 p.m. Titled California Connections, the concert is part of the California Festival: A Celebration of New Music, and will weave the music of Berkeley composers with those they have mentored and influenced in their work. The performance will embrace the healing sounds of Andean folk music through Gabriela Lena Frank’s Kanto Kechua No. 2 and uncover the majestic beauty of the Eastern Sierra Mountains in Ben Shirley’s High Sierra Sonata. Berkeley High School Alum Anaís Azul’s Cascades and Canyons will transport audiences through the serenity and challenges of nature, while Gabriella Smith’s Carrot Revolution inspires new perspectives through historical references. Also being performed are selections from John Adams’s rhythmic Book of Alleged Dances. Tickets are available at berkeleysymphony.org or by calling the box office at 510.841.2800. The concert will be performed by Julia Churchill, violin; Sarah Elert, violin; Alexandra Simpson, viola; Michael Graham, cello; Michel Taddei, double bass; Stacey Pelinka, flute; Roman Fukshansky, clarinet; and Britton Day, piano. The concert is part of over 100 performances in California through the Festival of New Music from November 3 to 19.
articles.title: Berkeley Symphony & Friends Chamber Music concert at PCA on Nov. 19

articles.text: Legacy of Love, a 2-part series of Retro and Mid-Century Jewelry from the collections of the Duchess of Windsor and Elizabeth Taylor (1935-1960s) will be held at Piedmont Center for the Arts starting on December 8. Jewelry from the 1930s-1960s is bold, colorful and extravagant. The Duchess of Windsor and Elizabeth Taylor each amassed what are considered today to be the best collections of jewelry from the 20th century. They both had amazing taste and a passion for important gemstones and innovative and avant-garde design. As the majority of their collections were gifts from their husbands, these collections are truly legacies of love. Both women led extraordinary lives that were very public. They were often vilified, criticized and at certain points in their lives portrayed as “the most hated women in the world” by the press. Prince of Wales Brooch, 1935 Wallis Simpson and Elizabeth Taylor The lectures by Piedmont resident and gemologist Sacha Grippando will examine these two exceptional ladies, their fascinating and scandalous lives, and of course their fabulous jewelry. The first of two parts, on Friday, December 8, will explore in depth the jewelry collection of Wallis Simpson, Duchess of Windsor. The second part is scheduled for Thursday evening, February 1, 2024. Both lectures will begin at 6 p.m. and will last a little more than one hour, to be followed by light refreshments. Donations are encouraged, and both events are open to all.
articles.title: Sacha Grippando presents A Legacy of Love at PCA

articles.text: Broken Embraces was written and directed by Pedro Almodovar, likely the best-known Spanish filmmaker of the last three decades. His most memorable film, at least in the U.S., was Volver (Return), and starred, as does Broken Embraces, Penelope Cruz, often referred to as Almodovar’s muse. It is unusual for male directors to explore and celebrate the resilience of women and their will to survive and even prevail. Volver is about women, young and old, women who are buffeted by the vagaries of life, by the inexplicable and by the unexpected. The narrative is compelling as are the complex characters. Broken Embraces is a love story with a strong woman at its center: the stunningly beautiful Elena (Penelope Cruz), who does what she must to carry on, to help her parents, even it means working as a discrete call girl and a secretary for a wealthy industrialist. Gradually she is pulled into a web of intrigue and duplicity and the film takes on a noirish tone as it moves from 2008 to 1994 in revealing flashbacks. The film is also completely taken with the transformative face of Elena/Cruz. She is shown in tight shots, pouting, smiling, making love, dressed in a variety of stylish clothes, at times looking like Audrey Hepburn or Marilyn Monroe. No doubt the camera loves Cruz and she loves it back. There are moments in the film when it feels like a Vogue layout, so lovely is she photographed. But as a story, constructed around intense relationships, a story that is convoluted and multilayered, it feels strangely detached. as if Almodovar cannot quite penetrate an abiding distance. It is perhaps because he is telling three stories simultaneously: one in 1994, another in 2008, and a third derived from the fact that there is a film within the film. Surprisingly, there are few if any moments in Broken Embraces when the characters reflect on the meaning of their actions. They are undisturbed by their choices and the narrative simply glides along in an undemanding way based on the assumption, presumably, that the filmgoer is not interested in knowing anything about the interior motivations of the characters. It is a missed opportunity by Almodovar to build intimacy with the audience; little is revealed. Even when the film is briefly set on two islands, Ibiza and Lanzarotte, Almodovar seems inclined only to use the lush scenery as a mere backdrop for Elena and her lover, Harry Cain (Luis Homar) and not as an extension of the heat of their relationship. If you love movies and have followed the career of Pedro Almodovar then Broken Embraces is a film not to be missed. pages.text: 18 Wednesday, November 15, 2023 MOVIE FOR ADULTS The Ghost Writer Ewan McGregor in The Ghost Writer By Chris Honoré I’m reluctant to say that The Ghost Writer is the antidote to those fast-paced, intense thrillers that are ever ubiquitous. articles.text: Part 5 in a series Because movies are so deeply embedded in our culture, we have included their titles and stories as familiar referents. Some are animated, others are portrayals of real life, both filled with a kind of magic. More than a few have become iconic. We are not as familiar with the countless behind-the-scenes individuals who write the narratives, create the characters, and oversee the productions. Watch the credits at the end of any film and you get a sense of the extraordinary number of people involved. Revealing who those people are and the depth of their talent has been the purpose of this series. In the Post’s search for community filmmakers, we discovered Katherine Sarafian. She grew up in San Leandro in an Armenian-American family. She attended San Leandro High School, and then enrolled at the University of California, Los Angeles, where she earned a Bachelor’s degree in communication studies followed by a Master’s degree in film and television critical studies. Aspired to be involved in the entertainment industry, Katherine joined Pixar Animation Studios in 1994, and began what continues to be a long and remarkable career. She was initially hired as an artist, but moved from the art department to marketing and soon became a film producer. In an article titled Adventures at Pixar Animation Studios, she describes the work of the producer: “From the outside the actor, director, screenwriter, and even the craft service person, all have obvious roles to play in the making of a movie, while the producer remains the behind-thescenes mastermind whose importance to the process few will ever Filmmaker Katherine Sarafian realize.” Regarding that process, for more than 20 years Katherine has been a part of almost every production at Pixar. Over the course of her career she has contributed to a panoply of the company’s much-acclaimed films, including the Oscar-winning animated feature Brave (2012), directed by Piedmont’s Mark Andrews, for which she was nominated for The Producer’s Guild Award for Outstanding Producer of an Animated Theatrical Motion Picture. Regarding her lengthy and fulfilling career at Pixar she commented, “I am still struck by how closely the company’s values are aligned with my own values and ethics. articles.text: A scene from Avatar with Sam Worthington and Zoe Saldana Avatar is breathtakingly beautiful, a science fiction/ fantasy hybrid that is unparalleled in its use of state-of-the-art technology – motion capture and CGI. It creates an alternative world that stirs a sense of wonder and awe from the first frame. James Cameron, the writer and director, lived with the nascent idea of Avatar for decades, waiting for cameras to be invented that could convey his vision. For the last four years, and employing some 2,000 people, he has worked relentlessly to bring to the screen what was once only a dream. As a visual spectacle, the film is glorious. As a story, it’s a gumbo of themes, stitched together in a narrative that takes more than two and half hours to develop. Essentially, the film is set on the distant moon of Pandora, inhabited by the Na’Vi – ten feet tall, with cat-like features and blue humanoid bodies. They are an aboriginal people with nothing more than bows and arrows; yet, they possess a profound connection to their natural world, a place of floating mountains, lush, luminescent forests filled with exotic animals and Paleolithic flying birds that they fearlessly ride. Their lives are filled with the sacred, and a natural wisdom that transcends the technology of those from earth who have arrived to mine a much-needed mineral called unobtanium. Earth, it seems, has finally been all but depleted of its resources (the year is 2154). The conundrum is that the Na’Vi live on the richest deposit of unobtanium on Pandora and must either be relocated peacefully or driven into the forest by force. A warrior and ex-Marine, Jake Sully (Sam Worthington), is melded with a Na’Vi body, created from their DNA, and sent to collect intel on the clan (hence the title Avatar). articles.text: New Orleans is one of the most unique cities on the planet. What is the best way to see this unique city and how many days do you need? First, let’s talk about what makes New Orleans so special. Society there is an easy-going friendship with all races, and Southern hospitality is truly exemplified. You need to know that Creole and Cajun are not synonymous. What is surprising is that, despite wide differences, there is a true meeting of the minds. The original inhabitants of the area were the indigenous tribes. French Canadians moved down the Mississippi and founded the city of New Orleans as a small community on the only high ground available. The original part of New Orleans known as the French Quarter is really tiny. Soon after, the Spanish arrived. The two groups sort of got along. With the arrival of the Americans, things got a little bit more difficult. And then in quick succession were the arrivals of Africans and people from every part of the Caribbean. The interesting thing is that, even though there was friction, the people found a way to work together which helped New Orleans develop in a unique way. The cuisine is completely unique. It is important to remember that there is a huge difference between Creole and Cajun. People who are Creole are people of mixed European and black descent, principally in the Caribbean. Cajuns are descendants of the early French-Canadian settlers. The gourmet in me was happy to enjoy both cuisines and I encourage you to do the same. Cajun and Creole restaurants abound. You can eat well almost anywhere. Restaurants identify themselves as either Cajun or Creole. This type of cooking was extremely popular a few years ago. Maybe you remember Justin Wilson and the guru of Louisiana cooking Paul Prudhomme. The latter wrote what is regarded as the bible of Louisiana cooking. If you don’t have this book, you should add it to your library. Breakfast is the least interesting meal of the day. Coffee roasted with chicory is the most common beverage. Beignets are popular, but ours were not very good; they were topped with a snow storm of powdered sugar. However, lunch and dinner were extraordinary. On Monday, everybody eats red beans and rice. articles.text: A group of 18 individuals met on November 6 for the monthly gathering of the First Mondays Reading Group. It had rained earlier in the day, but the afternoon was pleasant. The readers moved chairs from inside the Community Center to the patio. The group’s usual discussion leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long were away, so Hilary Honore, who had suggested The Trees for this month’s discussion, led the conversation. The book is a 2021 novel by American author Percival Everett and was shortlisted for the 2022 Booker Prize. The story is set mostly in the small town of Money, Mississippi, and follows a series of murders that have an identical pattern. A white man named Junior Junior is found dead with the body of an unknown Black man beside him. When the bodies are taken to the morgue it is discovered that the Black man’s body has disappeared. However, the same body is found again in the home of Junior Junior’s cousin, Wheat, who has also been murdered, and the body of the Black man soon disappears again, too. Two Black detectives from the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation, Ed Morgan and Jim Davis, are sent to Money to investigate the murders. They go to a bar frequented by members of the Black community and discover that both Junior and Wheat were relatives of Carolyn Bryant, a white woman who accused the teenage Emmett Till of making sexual advances towards her leading to his brutal 1955 murder. Ed and Jim believe the disappearing body resembles that of the battered Emmett Till. More bodies begin to appear around the country. Each is a white man who has been castrated and has the body of a Black or Asian man beside him. The detectives identify the Black man’s body found at the original crime scene, and they trace it to a company that sells bodies for research. They also suspect that Gertrude Penstock, a mixed-race person who passes for being white, and her 105-year-old great-grandmother, Mama Z, are involved in the murders. Gertrude and a group of like-minded Black people are suspected of having murdered Wheat and Junior Junior as retaliation for their father’s part in murdering Emmett Till. But the detectives are baffled by the other murders. There now are reports of other murders around the country by large groups of Black and Asian men. Bullets have no effect on them, and they are duplicating the murders orchestrated by Mama Z and Gertrude. The Trees was another great selection by the reading group; some readers loved it, while others couldn’t stand it. Those on the positive side said the book made them think about our nation’s history. There were over 800 counties in the U.S. where lynching occurred and where racial violence continues today. Percival Everett wants us to understand that not much has changed. Everett’s storytelling is often humorous and sometimes over the top, but this is a serious subject. Some felt guilty when laughing at the sad events in the book. Others felt this serious, tragic situation was handled too frivolously. The idea of how terrible each murder was didn’t come across for them. Some readers enjoyed the creativity and humor in the first part of the book, but the enjoyment fell off for them later. The presentation of most of the white characters as being backward, stupid, and bad didn’t seem realistic or balanced. Some readers found the ending with large groups of zombies unsatisfying and the many murders became repetitious. Perhaps that’s how Percival Everett and Black people feel about what they experience in their lives. The readers questioned how it feels to be threatened all the time. There was a lot to discuss and agree or disagree about. The readers did agree they would not have read The Trees if not for the First Mondays Reading Group, and they were pleased to be a part of it. The group had previously selected The Finest Hours by Michael J. Tougias and Casey Sherman for December, and Station Eleven by Canadian writer Emily St. John Mandel for their January read. For February the group picked The Code Breaker by Walter Isaacson. The group’s next discussion will be on December 4 at 1:30 p.m. at Piedmont Community Hall in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome to join the group and there is no fee, Registration is required at https://bit. ly/3R86PP4.

articles.text: It’s hard to imagine a comedy based on the Holocaust, but the brilliant Italian comic Roberto Begnini not only imagined one, he wrote it, directed it, and starred in it. It went on to win the top prize at the Cannes Film Festival and picked up three 1997 Academy Awards as well, including Best Foreign Film and Best Actor. It’s called Life Is Beautiful (La vita é bella), and last week the audience at Piedmont’s Second Thursday Film Fest got to check it out. It’s set in the 1940s, when fascism had taken firm hold in Italy and the nation had formed an alliance with both Mussolini and Hitler. Italy also began persecuting Jews big time, establishing internment camps of its own. As the movie begins, the crisis point, when Northern Italy was occupied by the Germans, has not yet been reached, so the first half of the tale delights us with a charming rom-com set in Arezzo, in which Guido Orefice, a clever young Jewish restaurant worker, uses his smarts to win a pretty Gentile girl named Dora away from her fiancé (he steals her from her engagement party on a horse). They marry, have a child, a boy, Giosué, and open a bookstore. And then the bad guys march in, and the family winds up on a train to an internment camp. There, Dora is separated from her husband and son, so the sole parent, Guido, uses all his wiles to keep his son from understanding and suffering from their plight. We’re amused by Guido’s tricks and hairsbreadth escapes, but the movie can’t hold the truth of the situation and its consequences at bay. Despite its honors and awards, Life Is Beautiful had its critics. Entertainment Weekly called it “the first feel-good Holocaust weepie,” and, surprisingly, Mel Brooks, who wrote The Producers, panned it. But the worldwide audience vote was overwhelmingly positive, and, enlightened by Darby Gragg’s excellent introduction, the Piedmont audience liked it, too. The next Film Fest showing, on December 14th, is the international comedy, Dirty Rotten Scoundrels from 1988, starring Michael Caine and Steve Martin. The Film Fest takes place in the Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue on the second Thursday of each month. Doors open at 10:15 a.m., with a showtime at 10:30. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration with the Recreation Department PRD is recommended at https:// bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Guests are welcome to bring snacks or lunch.

articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays wanted to see some streets they hadn’t gone to this year, so they headed for Rose and Kingston Avenues. They are some of Piedmont’s earliest streets with some beautiful Victorians, including some built prior to 1900. A turnout of 40 walkers and three K-9 arrived for the walk. The group crossed Grand Avenue and climbed Greenbank up to Rose Avenue where they enjoyed seeing Rose’s many old homes that were built the early 1900s, especially three Victorians. It was noted that the homes on the south side of Kingston are in Piedmont and those on the north side are in Oakland. The walkers went down to Linda Avenue and crossed it to go up Kingston. 780 was the former home of walker Meghan Bennett. Research by Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombard provided its story and also that of the house next door at 778. These two homes were built in 1892 by William Vickery and his sister, Elizabeth Vickery Hadden at costs of $4,300 and $3,300. They were the first homes on this street that was then called Summit Avenue. The houses were built in the fashionable shingle style of the 1890s. The backyard of the house at 778 is one of the deepest lots in Piedmont going back 150 feet, The entire lot is 220 feet deep. Google Maps shows the backyard of the home at 784 is even deeper. Neighborhood lore says the houses at 778 and 784 once shared a kitchen and the two families ate their meals together. Nancy DeRoche urged the group to go a little further up Kingston to see a historic brick home. It was designed by Albert Farr and built in 1908. An iron gate blocks the driveway entrance with the house further back. As the group was peeking through the gate, the owner, Chad Olcott, happened to be coming out and saw the group. Chad, who owns Mulberry’s Market in Piedmont, invited the walkers to come in for a tour of the house. The group noticed that there is also a chicken coop with live chickens just inside the gate. Chad said he once had ducks too. Showing great hospitality, he took the walkers through the house, and shared the stories of buying the house, rebuilding part of it, and remodeling much of it. The home is lovely and has a wonderful historical feel. The front of the house was also a great spot for a group photo with Chad, who later shared an early photo of the house. It was time for the group to make a direct return to the Exedra. They went back on Kingston to Linda, past Beach School, and on to Grand, Wildwood, and Magnolia Avenues, and finally to the Exedra. It was an almost four-mile walk on a beautiful, fall morning with an unexpected treat from Chad Olcott that was enjoyed and appreciated by all. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Credited with saving Piedmont Boy Scout Council Carl West Anderson died peacefully on November 4, 2023 in Reno, Nevada after complications from a fall. A man of strong passion, devotion, and honor, he tackled life with enthusiasm, hard work, and love. Carl was born on September 11, 1935, in Monterey Park, California and grew up in Albany. He attended Cal, and after graduating in 1957, he completed six months of active duty as a second lieutenant in the U.S. Army Reserve. He returned to academia at UC Berkeley to attend Boalt Hall School of Law. Upon graduation, he was awarded a one-year fellowship to study with a German judge. Fortuitously, on the way to his internship in Germany, he visited Amsterdam where he met Margo at the Rijksmuseum. He returned home to serve as a deputy district attorney for Alameda County, was assigned to the Berkeley office, and married Margo. During his nine years as deputy district attorney, he was sent to Sacramento to lobby for the California District Attorneys Association, the California Peace Officers Association, and the California State Sheriffs Association. Governor Reagan appointed him to the Alameda County Superior Court on the last day of his term. The appointment was Carl Anderson in his back yard with his dog Lola. Retired First District California Court of Appeal Administrative Presiding Justice Carl Anderson died on November 4 at age 87. challenged by the new governor, but was subsequently confirmed. After nine years on the California Superior Court, Governor George Deukmejian appointed him a justice of the First District California Court of Appeal in San Francisco where he eventually became Administrative Presiding Justice. During his tenure, his court became a pilot court for the American Bar Association’s (ABA) project on appellate court delay reduction. Over the course of seven years, the court completely eliminated what had been a historical two-to-five-year backlog of appeals. During this period, Judge Anderson was active with the ABA and the Council of Chief Judges of the Courts of Appeal, encouraging all intermediate federal and U.S. state appellate courts to adopt time standards for processing their appeals. After retiring from the court in 1997, he worked for 23 years as a neutral arbitrator and mediator, affiliated with the American Arbitration Association. Carl’s passion for his community was demonstrated by his long involvement with the Piedmont Scout Council. He is credited with leading the effort to prevent the Piedmont Scout Council from being absorbed into larger councils and to retain its independence as one of the smallest councils in the U.S. Judge Anderson was also involved with the Rotary Club of Oakland, the Lake Merritt Breakfast Club, Volunteers of America of the Bay Area, Piedmont Educational Foundation, Piedmont Beautification Foundation, Piedmont Community Church, and his neighborhood utility undergrounding project. The family suggests that memorial donations in lieu of flowers may be made to any of those organizations or to the charity of your choice. A memorial service will be held at 10:30 a.m. on Friday, November 17 at Piedmont Community Church, with a reception immediately following. An avid gardener, he served on the UC Botanical Gardens Board of Directors and cultivated a beautiful native Sierra garden. He is predeceased by Margo Hart, his loving wife of 53 years. He is survived by his son, Thomas, his daughter-in-law Susan, granddaughter Samantha, daughter Marnie, and son-in-law Will. Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03

Piedmont Real Estate Update November 2023 Seasonality in the Bay Area Real Estate Market As we’ve seen over the past few years, the real estate market in our area is a dynamic and ever-changing landscape. While you might not think certain seasons weigh on the amount you’re paying or asking for your home — they do! There can be a difference as high as 10% in some cases. [Source: National Association of Realtors.] Understanding the ebb and flow throughout the year is crucial for buyers and sellers. In this month’s newsletter, we’ll explore how different seasons affect the real estate market and what you can do to position yourself strategically. The Spring Market in the Bay Area — New Listings and High Demand It’s well known that certain times of the year can be more active than others, filled with either benefits or challenges, depending on your place in the process. Spring is typically a popular time to look for a new home because buyers have been waiting out the slow winter months for new inventory, and sellers have been priming for the best conditions to showcase their home — think sunshine and pretty gardens. These two factors mean it all starts with a bang in early spring and peaks in late spring/early summer. As a seller, spring can be an excellent opportunity for bustling buyer activity and the potential for multiple offers. But from a buyer’s perspective, you’re part of a bigger pool of buyers, which can translate into increased competition, multiple offers, and higher prices. Our strong market continues through June and July, usually showing some slowing in August. The fall season, once school is back in session, can be an excellent time to sell. Especially here in the Bay Area with our lovely Indian Summer weather. It’s a little less frenzied than spring and offers the opportunity to complete the sale before the holidays. For the buyers who have the drive and interest to keep looking through the winter season, it just might pay off. Sellers can’t always follow the market’s seasonality, and you might find a great opportunity with little competition.
